promises.claim: What’s Missing names headshots first when you have none, since every submission starts with one.
Permission To Work on the Overview is the same permission Papers shows under Permission To Work.
Your résumé uses your professional name, and one made under another name reads as behind.
Your special skills are your techniques on the Player Profile, at the level it shows.
Once you have headshots, What’s Missing stops asking for them, until they’re more than two years old.
The session’s price comes out of your bank as a work cost.
Once you have a résumé, What’s Missing stops asking for one, until your record moves on past it.
A School production’s part goes on your résumé once its run has closed.
A self-tape of a practice brief is the first recorded work a reel can be cut from.
Once you have a reel, What’s Missing stops asking for one, and says when newer work came after it.
A check refuses an approach with no headshots, since every submission starts with one.
A check refuses an approach with no résumé, and a résumé behind your record is one thing his office can ask for.
Sending your materials puts his office’s answer on the way, about ${TIME_WORDS.reply} on.
A meeting kept or missed, and material sent when asked, are read under Reliability.
A meeting stops the clock like any commitment, and offers Ask To Move at the stop.
Your reel’s best band is part of Your Work, and a reel is part of Stage And Screen.
Each answer his office gives keeps its reasons here.
Signing with him gives no permission to work: Papers, under Permission To Work, still says what you may do.
Accepting, declining and the agreement’s end each go in History With His Office.
Each payment lands in your account on its payday, or from your agency’s trust account a few business days later.
Your tax return reads each payment’s wages, withholding, commission, dues and the town the work was done in.
Each engagement’s dates are read against your permission to work when you book it.
Commission comes off your pay as it passes through your agency’s trust account.
The year’s commission counts toward the performing artist’s deduction the return works out.
Each union bill comes out of your bank on its day.
Your résumé lists your unions once you’re a member.
Dues count toward the cost of your work on the year’s return.
A submission starts with your headshots: without them it can’t be sent.
A submission puts the casting office’s answer on the clock, and the answer sets an audition.
Casting reads your audition’s band, with the role’s fit and the field, when it decides whether to offer you the role.
An audition in person goes on your calendar with its trip, and stops the clock when it comes.
An offer can be accepted only where your permission to work covers every one of its days.
The part goes on your professional credits, and your résumé reads as behind until it has it.
Accepting puts each work day on your calendar, and each stops the clock for you.
Work in term without approval moves your standing to academic warning, and a second time to dismissal.
An offer in term is accepted on the School’s approval, or against it with the warning said first.
Your two scenes become pieces of coursework, each prepared with its own steps.
Each scene’s note comes at its first showcase day, and Los Angeles shows whether you took it.
An Incomplete still open at the end of the ${TERM_WEEK} keeps you out of the showcase.
How each scene went at each showcase day stays on your professional record.
